SIDEBAR:
### How to use this page

#### You need
A CSV file of your team's work items. A Jira export works with no changes.

To export from Jira: Filters › Export › CSV (all fields). The tool skips open items. The file can be up to 10 MB.

#### Steps
1. Choose the sample file (an example team) or upload your file.
2. Enter how many work items are left (backlog). Do not count bugs or epics.
3. Read the dates in the result.
4. Copy the message to your sponsor.

#### Which date to use
- **50% chance of completion (P50):** use it to plan your own work.
- **85% chance of completion (P85):** use it for the date you give a sponsor or client.
- **95% chance of completion (P95):** use it when a late finish costs a lot.
- **Velocity date:** use it to compare with your sprint plan. It uses your team's average pace in story points. If you do not enter the story points left in More options, the tool estimates them.

#### Be careful
The dates assume your team keeps its recent pace (throughput).

The 85% date can be too early. See "How accurate is it?" on the page.

#### Privacy
The tool uses your file only for this forecast. It does not store the file or show issue keys.

how_it_works:
[Part(title='How the dates are made (Monte Carlo)', body="The tool does not use one average pace. It replays your team's real good days and bad days many times.

1. Count how many work items the team finished on each of the last 84 days.
2. Make one try: for each future day, pick one of those past days at random and use its count.
3. Add the counts until all the work left is done. That day is the finish date of this try.
4. Do 10,000 tries. Each try gives a different finish date.
5. Sort the finish dates. The 50% date (P50) is the day by which half of the tries finish. The 85% (P85) and 95% (P95) dates work the same way. Give the 85% date (P85) to your sponsor or client.

Story points are not needed for these dates. The velocity date uses story points, for comparison."), Part(title='How accurate is it? (back-test: the 85% date was too early about 1 in 3 times)', body='We tested the tool on the history of 29 real open-source projects. A forecast is one prediction of when the next 10, 25 or 50 work items (not bugs or epics) will be done.

1. Pick a past date in a project. Use only the work done up to that date.
2. Make the forecast.
3. Compare it with the date the work was really done.

- **7,692** past forecasts checked (**903** more had too little history to forecast)
- **69 of 100** done by the 85% date (target: 75 to 95 of 100)
- **About 1 in 3** finished later than the 85% date

So the 85% date is often too early. Use the 95% date when a late finish costs a lot. The result is published as it is, although it missed the target.')]
